Family Health

Endometrial cancer: symptoms, stages, treatment and risk factors

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Endometrial cancer starts in the lining of the uterus. Unusual vaginal bleeding is often its first sign, which can lead to diagnosis while the cancer is still at an early stage. Prompt assessment matters, but bleeding or pelvic pain does not automatically mean cancer. Understanding the tests and treatment choices can help you take part in decisions about your care.

What endometrial cancer is

The endometrium is the tissue lining the inside of the uterus. During the reproductive years, it changes in response to hormones and is shed during menstruation when pregnancy does not occur. Endometrial cancer develops when cells in this lining begin to grow without normal control.

It is the most common form of uterine cancer. It is different from uterine sarcoma, which arises in muscle or supporting tissues, and from cancer that begins in the cervix. Those distinctions matter because testing, treatment and outlook can differ.

Many cases can be treated successfully, especially when found early. Nevertheless, the diagnosis alone does not tell you how one person will do. The type of cancer, its extent, laboratory findings, health and response to treatment all contribute.

Symptoms that should be checked

The most frequent warning sign is a change in vaginal bleeding: periods that become unusually heavy or prolonged, spotting between periods, or any bleeding after menopause. Report even a small amount of postmenopausal spotting rather than waiting for it to become heavier.

Other possible symptoms include watery or blood-stained discharge, pain low in the abdomen or pelvis, discomfort during sex, or painful or difficult urination. These symptoms can have other causes, including benign uterine or vaginal conditions.

Changes around menopause can affect bleeding, but unexplained bleeding should not simply be attributed to the menopause without assessment. If bleeding continues or returns after an initial reassuring result, contact the clinician again.

Heavy bleeding with faintness, collapse or severe pelvic pain needs emergency assessment. Otherwise, arrange a prompt appointment to establish the cause and next steps. You do not need to decide for yourself whether the symptoms sound like cancer before seeking help.

Examination, ultrasound and tissue sampling

The clinician will ask about your symptoms, medicines, menstrual or menopause history, previous illnesses and family history. A pelvic examination can help identify changes in the reproductive organs and other potential sources of bleeding.

A transvaginal ultrasound uses a slender probe placed in the vagina to create images with sound waves. It can assess the uterine lining and look for structural changes. Ultrasound findings alone do not always settle whether cancer is present.

An endometrial biopsy takes a small tissue sample, often through a thin tube passed through the cervix. A pathologist examines it in the laboratory. Hysteroscopy uses a narrow viewing instrument to inspect the uterine cavity and can guide sampling of a suspicious area.

Dilation and curettage, or D&C, involves opening the cervix and obtaining tissue from inside the uterus. It may be used when another sample is insufficient or further evaluation is needed. Ask how discomfort will be managed and what to expect before consenting to a procedure.

Biopsy is not reserved only for an abnormal ultrasound. ACOG’s April 2026 guidance recommends ultrasound together with tissue sampling in the initial assessment of most people with postmenopausal bleeding. The plan should reflect the person’s circumstances and shared decision-making.

If cancer is confirmed, additional assessment helps determine its extent. Depending on the situation, this can involve imaging, blood tests and information obtained at surgery. Keep copies of the pathology and scan reports, particularly if requesting a second opinion.

Understanding stages I to IV

A stage describes how the cancer is classified at diagnosis and helps guide care. Broadly, stage I represents early disease, usually limited to the uterus; stage II includes certain more extensive local findings; stage III involves local or regional spread; and stage IV includes involvement of the bladder or bowel lining or more distant spread.

Older explanations describe stage II mainly as spread into the cervix and stage III as involvement of nearby tissues, ovaries, tubes, vagina or regional lymph nodes. Those descriptions remain useful background, but they are not a complete guide to current staging.

The 2023 FIGO system also incorporates features such as cancer type, invasion of small lymph or blood vessels and some molecular findings. It has selected exceptions, including some low-grade cancers involving the uterus and an ovary that can be classified as early disease. A stage cannot safely be assigned from a short checklist.

Ask which staging system your team uses, the full stage and substage, and which findings led to it. Stage affects treatment and prognosis, but it is considered alongside the pathology and your health, not in isolation.

Cancer type, grade and molecular findings

Most endometrial cancers arise from gland-forming tissue and are called adenocarcinomas. Endometrioid carcinoma is the most common. Other groups include serous, clear-cell, mixed, undifferentiated or dedifferentiated cancers and carcinosarcoma, as well as rare forms requiring specialist classification.

You may encounter the older terms type 1 and type 2. Type 1 generally referred to more common, often estrogen-related endometrioid cancers, while type 2 included more aggressive forms such as serous cancer. This two-group description is too broad to determine an individual treatment plan.

Grade describes microscopic features of the tumor and is different from stage. Molecular testing can provide additional information, with groups including POLE-mutated, mismatch-repair-deficient, p53-abnormal and tumors without a specific molecular profile.

These results can help estimate recurrence risk and guide treatment. Ask for an explanation in everyday language; recognizing a subtype name does not mean you should infer the outlook or choose a drug yourself.

Making a treatment plan

Treatment is planned with a specialist cancer team, often including a gynecologic oncologist. The recommendation depends on stage, cancer type and grade, molecular or receptor findings, other health conditions and your preferences.

Ask what each treatment aims to achieve, the likely benefits, important side effects and alternatives. Some people need surgery alone, while others need several treatments. A combination is not automatically better for every diagnosis.

Tell the team early if future pregnancy is important to you. Ask about fertility advice before treatment starts, because surgery, radiation and medicines can affect reproductive options. Fertility-preserving care is appropriate only for selected situations.

Surgery and lymph-node assessment

Surgery commonly involves a hysterectomy to remove the uterus, usually including the cervix. Removing both fallopian tubes and ovaries is called bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and is often part of the same cancer operation. The exact procedure should be explained beforehand.

The team may also assess lymph nodes to help determine whether cancer has spread. This does not always mean removing every nearby node: sentinel-node mapping and biopsy can be used in suitable cases, while other findings may require a different approach.

If cancer extends beyond the uterus, additional surgery may sometimes be considered. The amount of surgery depends on the location and extent of disease and whether the expected benefits justify the risks.

Hysterectomy means you can no longer carry a pregnancy. Removing the ovaries before natural menopause also changes hormone production. Discuss these consequences, recovery and symptom management with the team rather than assuming that all operations have identical effects.

Radiation treatment

Radiation uses high-energy treatment to damage cancer cells in a defined area. External-beam radiation comes from a machine outside the body. Brachytherapy places a radiation source through an applicator close to the area being treated, often the upper vagina after surgery.

One form or a combination may be recommended, commonly after surgery to reduce the risk of cancer returning locally. Less often, radiation is used before surgery to help shrink a tumor. If surgery is unsuitable because of health or other circumstances, radiation may be the main treatment.

The plan depends on the actual diagnosis and treatment goal. Ask about fatigue, bowel or bladder symptoms, vaginal changes and longer-term effects, as well as how to report problems. Treatment schedules and supportive measures should come from your radiation team.

Chemotherapy and newer drug treatments

Chemotherapy uses medicines that affect cancer cells. It may involve one drug or a combination and is commonly delivered through a vein for endometrial cancer. The medicines and schedule depend on the treatment plan; not every cancer medicine taken by mouth is chemotherapy.

It can be used when cancer has spread, has returned after earlier treatment, or when features of a newly diagnosed cancer indicate that additional treatment is appropriate. Sometimes it is combined or sequenced with radiation.

Modern treatment can also include immunotherapy or targeted medicines in selected settings. Tumor testing and previous treatment can influence which options are suitable. Their availability and approved uses change, so a current specialist plan is more useful than a fixed list of drugs in a general article.

Ask which side effects need an immediate call, who to contact outside office hours and whether a clinical trial is relevant. Do not change or stop prescribed cancer treatment based on general information.

Hormonal treatment and preserving fertility

Hormonal treatment uses hormones or medicines that alter hormone action to slow suitable cancers. It is different from hormone therapy used to relieve menopause symptoms. Progestins are one important group, but there are other approaches.

It may be considered for selected advanced or recurrent cancers, particularly some lower-grade, slower-growing tumors with hormone receptors. It is not confined to stages III and IV, and it is not automatically combined with chemotherapy.

A small group with carefully assessed early, low-grade endometrioid cancer may be considered for hormonal treatment that temporarily preserves the uterus. This requires specialist selection, exclusion of more extensive disease and close repeat assessment. It is not a general alternative to recommended surgery.

Discuss how response will be measured, what would trigger a change in treatment and the plan after pregnancy or if the cancer does not respond. Keeping the uterus during treatment does not guarantee a future pregnancy or remove the need for cancer follow-up.

Age, hormone exposure and reproductive history

Risk generally increases with age and the disease is most common after menopause, although younger people can develop it. US registry information places most diagnoses between ages 45 and 74; that is a population pattern, not an age range outside which symptoms can be ignored.

Longer exposure of the lining to estrogen without enough progesterone effect can increase risk. An early first period, later menopause and never having been pregnant are associated with higher risk. None means that a person will inevitably develop cancer, and pregnancy should not be pursued as cancer prevention.

PCOS can increase risk, particularly when ovulation is infrequent and the lining is not regularly exposed to progesterone. It is inaccurate to assume that every person with PCOS has the same continuously high estrogen measurement.

Some estrogen-producing ovarian tumors, including granulosa-cell tumors, can also stimulate the uterine lining. These are specific medical conditions requiring their own assessment. Risk factors are clues for care, not a way to diagnose cancer from personal history.

Menopause therapy, tamoxifen and contraception

Systemic estrogen treatment for menopause can increase endometrial cancer risk when used without adequate progestogen protection in someone who still has a uterus. Discuss the formulation and whether protection is needed with the prescriber; not all local and systemic products have the same considerations.

Tamoxifen can act differently in breast and uterine tissue. It is valuable for preventing or treating certain breast cancers but can increase endometrial cancer risk. Its benefits often outweigh that risk. Report abnormal bleeding and discuss concerns rather than stopping it yourself.

Oral contraceptives are associated with a lower risk of endometrial cancer. Intrauterine contraceptive use has also been associated with lower risk, but a device is not a guarantee against cancer or a substitute for investigating bleeding.

Each option has benefits and possible harms beyond the endometrium. A clinician can help choose contraception or menopause care that fits your health and preferences. Do not start medication solely to reduce a statistical cancer risk without that discussion.

Endometrial hyperplasia is not all the same

Endometrial hyperplasia means overgrowth of the uterine lining. It is not automatically cancer, but the laboratory classification matters. Hyperplasia without atypia differs from atypical hyperplasia or endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, often shortened to EIN, which is a precancerous condition.

Abnormal bleeding is a common reason it is discovered. Some non-atypical changes may settle or respond to treatment, but a diagnosis should come with a clear follow-up plan. It is unsafe to assume that all hyperplasia will disappear on its own.

Treatment can involve progestin, delivered in an appropriate oral or intrauterine form, rather than simply generic hormone replacement therapy. For EIN or atypical hyperplasia, hysterectomy is the definitive treatment; when surgery is not chosen or is unsuitable, clinicians first assess for coexisting cancer and arrange progestin treatment with close surveillance.

Ask what the biopsy actually showed, how much concern there is about progression or an already present cancer, and when repeat assessment is needed. A scan reporting a thick lining is not identical to a tissue diagnosis of hyperplasia.

Body weight, diabetes and metabolic health

Higher body fat is associated with greater endometrial cancer risk. Fat tissue can convert other hormones into estrogen, which is one reason the relationship matters, particularly after menopause. This association does not identify the cause of cancer in an individual.

Type 2 diabetes and related metabolic conditions are also associated with increased risk. Their relationships with body weight, insulin and other factors overlap. It is misleading to give everyone with diabetes or a particular BMI one fixed multiplier for their personal chance of cancer.

Support with blood-glucose management, physical activity and sustainable weight-related goals can benefit overall health. Cancer is not evidence that someone failed at self-care. Continue appropriate medical assessment regardless of weight or diabetes status.

Family history and Lynch syndrome

Tell the clinician if close relatives have had endometrial or bowel cancer, especially at younger ages, or if the family has a known inherited cancer syndrome. Lynch syndrome involves inherited changes in DNA mismatch-repair pathways and raises the risk of several cancers, including endometrial and colorectal cancer.

The level of risk differs according to the gene and family circumstances. A single lifetime figure such as 40–60% should not be applied to everyone with Lynch syndrome. Genetic counseling can clarify what a result means and whether relatives should consider testing.

Risk-reducing hysterectomy and possible removal of the tubes and ovaries may be discussed after childbearing. Timing and whether to remove the ovaries require an individual discussion about the gene, age, family history, health, menopause effects and preferences; surgery is not an automatic response to any family history.

A previous breast or ovarian cancer should also be mentioned because shared risk factors, inherited susceptibility or treatments may affect assessment. Prior radiation to the pelvis is another relevant part of the history. Not every cancer survivor has the same risk.

Why cells become cancerous

For many people, there is no single identifiable cause. Hormonal stimulation can promote growth of the endometrial lining, but a thick lining or a hormone imbalance is not by itself cancer.

Changes in the genes that control cell growth, repair and survival can allow cells to multiply abnormally and form a tumor. Some susceptibility is inherited, while many changes arise in the tumor itself. Not all endometrial cancers are driven by estrogen in the same way.

Researchers continue to study how these processes interact. This is why cancer type and molecular findings provide information that a list of risk factors alone cannot supply.

Steps that may lower risk

There is no guaranteed way to prevent endometrial cancer. Regular physical activity and support toward a sustainable, healthy weight may lower risk and have broader health benefits. The effect for a particular person cannot be promised.

Have unexplained bleeding assessed and follow the treatment and monitoring plan for hyperplasia or EIN. Discuss the endometrial effects of menopause treatment and the wider benefits and risks of contraceptive options when choosing them.

If Lynch syndrome is suspected or confirmed, ask for a specialist prevention and follow-up plan. Do not rely on routine cervical screening for reassurance: a Pap or HPV test is not an endometrial cancer screening test.

There is no standard routine screening program for average-risk people without symptoms. Investigating bleeding is different from screening a person who feels well, and higher inherited risk requires an individualized approach.

Putting survival statistics in context

For context, current US SEER data estimate a lifetime uterine-cancer risk of about 3.1%, based on 2021–2023 data. The reported five-year relative survival for uterine cancer is 80.9%, using diagnoses from 2016–2022. These statistics cover a registry category broader than a single endometrial subtype.

Relative survival compares survival in people with cancer with what would be expected in a comparable population. It is not a statement that treatment guarantees five years of life, nor does it mean that someone who reaches five years cannot live much longer.

Outcomes are generally better when disease is found earlier, but stage, cancer biology and treatment response matter. Ask the oncology team to explain the information relevant to your diagnosis rather than applying an all-stage average to yourself.

Emotional support and preparing for care

Fear, sadness, uncertainty or difficulty coping can accompany diagnosis and treatment. Tell the team how you are managing emotionally as well as physically. Support can include counseling, an oncology social worker or other mental-health care.

Some people find an in-person or online cancer support group helpful; others prefer individual conversations. Choose the kind of support that feels useful to you. Practical help with appointments, work, family responsibilities and communicating with loved ones can also reduce the burden.

For an appointment, write down your symptoms, medicines and questions. Ask for the diagnosis, stage, treatment goal and follow-up plan in writing, and bring a trusted person if you wish. Raise concerns about pain, fertility, menopause or sexual health so they can be addressed alongside the cancer treatment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Unexplained vaginal bleeding, especially after menopause, requires assessment even when there may be a benign cause.

Tissue sampling establishes the diagnosis; a reassuring ultrasound alone is not always sufficient. April 2026 ACOG guidance supports combined initial assessment for most postmenopausal bleeding.

Modern classification considers tumor type, grade and molecular information as well as anatomical spread. Ask which staging system is being used.

Treatment and inherited-risk counseling are individualized. General information should not be used to select, stop or postpone cancer treatment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains the language used in cancer care and helps you prepare for conversations. Decisions about diagnosis, staging, medicines, surgery and fertility-preserving treatment belong in a current specialist care plan.

When to seek help

Arrange prompt assessment of unexpected bleeding or persistent pelvic symptoms. Any bleeding after menopause should be checked. Heavy bleeding with faintness or severe pain needs emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Abnormal bleeding is the most common warning sign, but symptoms alone do not diagnose cancer.
  • Biopsy and appropriate follow-up matter, including when an ultrasound is reassuring.
  • Stage, grade and cancer type describe different aspects of the diagnosis.
  • Hyperplasia without atypia and EIN or atypical hyperplasia need different levels of concern and follow-up.
  • Discuss fertility wishes before treatment and medication concerns before making changes.
  • Population survival figures cannot predict an individual outcome; emotional and practical support are part of care.

Frequently asked questions

What are the main symptoms of endometrial cancer?

Unexpected vaginal bleeding, including heavier or longer periods, bleeding between periods or any bleeding after menopause, is the most common sign. Watery or blood-stained discharge, pelvic pain or pain during sex can also occur. These symptoms need assessment but do not necessarily mean cancer.

Is endometrial hyperplasia the same as cancer?

No. It means overgrowth of the lining, but the tissue findings matter. Hyperplasia without atypia differs from EIN or atypical hyperplasia, which is precancerous and needs an appropriate treatment and surveillance plan. Generic menopause HRT is not the standard answer for hyperplasia.

What causes endometrial cancer?

There is often no single identifiable cause. Changes controlling cell growth and repair can lead to cancer. Prolonged estrogen stimulation contributes to some forms, while other cancers have different biology. Risk factors do not prove what caused one person’s disease.

Can I lower my risk?

Regular activity, supported weight and metabolic-health care, assessment of abnormal bleeding, and appropriate treatment of precancer can help. Discuss hormone or contraceptive choices with your clinician. None guarantees prevention, and inherited risk needs specialist advice.

Does a normal ultrasound rule it out?

Not always. Tissue sampling may still be needed. ACOG’s 2026 update recommends ultrasound plus endometrial sampling in the initial assessment of most people with postmenopausal bleeding. Persistent or returning symptoms should be reported even after reassuring initial tests.

Are stage and grade the same?

No. Stage classifies the extent and, in newer systems, selected additional features of the cancer. Grade describes microscopic characteristics. Molecular findings can add further information. Ask your team to explain each part of your own pathology and staging report.

Does everyone need chemotherapy?

No. Some people need surgery alone, while others benefit from radiation, chemotherapy or other medicines. The combination depends on the cancer’s extent and biology, the person’s health and the goals of treatment.

Can fertility be preserved?

Sometimes, for carefully selected early, low-grade endometrioid cancers under specialist care. Hormonal treatment with close surveillance may temporarily preserve the uterus. It is not suitable for everyone and does not guarantee pregnancy. Raise fertility wishes before starting treatment.

Should I stop tamoxifen or menopause treatment?

Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own. Discuss your symptoms, uterine status and individual risks with the prescriber. Tamoxifen’s breast-cancer benefits often outweigh its uterine risk, while menopause-treatment choices depend on the formulation and need for endometrial protection.

What does a five-year survival figure mean?

It describes outcomes in a group over a defined period, usually relative to expected survival in a comparable population. It is not an expiry date or a personal prediction. Your own outlook depends on stage, cancer biology, health and response to treatment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
